question: Why is taking a detailed work history essential when evaluating a patient with chronic respiratory symptoms?

options.A: It helps determine the exact financial compensation the worker deserves from employers
options.B: It reveals whether the patient has a family history of congenital pulmonary anomalies
options.C: It establishes the precise viral strain responsible for acute upper respiratory infections
options.D: It links ongoing lung damage to specific hazardous exposures in the workplace environment

explanation: Because occupational lung diseases closely mimic other respiratory illnesses, identifying specific workplace toxins is vital for an accurate diagnosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which particle size range is most likely to reach the terminal bronchioles and alveoli during inhalation?
explanation: Finer particles within this specific size range bypass the upper airway defenses and penetrate deep into the gas-exchange regions of the lung. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary cellular mechanism that leads to fibrosis following silica dust deposition?

options.A: Direct calcification of the pulmonary arterial walls due to mineral absorption
options.B: Destruction of alveolar macrophages releasing enzymes that stimulate collagen production
options.C: Massive accumulation of watery fluid within the pleural cavity spaces
options.D: Rapid replication of ciliated epithelial cells lining the major bronchi

explanation: When macrophages fail to digest toxic dusts, they break down and release chemicals that activate fibroblasts to form scar tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h2)

question: What defines pneumoconiosis among occupational respiratory disorders?

options.A: Acute pulmonary edema caused by accidental chlorine gas leakage
options.B: Reversible bronchospasm caused by chemical irritant exposure
options.C: Granulomatous lung inflammation triggered by organic fungal spores
options.D: Fibrotic lung changes resulting from the inhalation of inorganic mineral dusts

explanation: Pneumoconioses are specifically caused by the tissue reaction to accumulated inorganic dusts like silica, coal, or asbestos. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h3)

question: How does hypersensitivity pneumonitis fundamentally differ in origin from simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis?

options.A: It develops within minutes of acute exposure rather than taking years to manifest clinically
options.B: It responds completely to routine bronchodilator therapy without requiring removal from exposure
options.C: It involves an immune-mediated allergic reaction to organic dusts rather than scarring from inorganic minerals
options.D: It causes complete destruction of the upper airway cartilage instead of affecting the alveoli

explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immunologic response to organic antigens, whereas pneumoconioses stem from inorganic dust accumulation and fibrosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h3)

question: Which occupational activity is most strongly associated with heavy exposure to crystalline silica dust in Nigeria?

options.A: Manual harvesting of cocoa pods on plantations
options.C: Artisanal gold mining and stone quarrying
options.D: Commercial deep-sea fishing along the coast

explanation: Quarrying and informal mining involve breaking rock and earth that release high concentrations of silica dust into the breathing zone. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h4)

question: A metal welder working in a poorly ventilated roadside workshop in a Nigerian urban center presents with respiratory complaints. What primary etiological agent is most likely responsible for their symptoms?

options.A: Cotton dust fibers accumulating in the terminal bronchioles
options.B: Toxic metal fumes generated during high-heat joining of metals
options.C: Asbestos micro-fibers shed from automotive brake linings
options.D: Fungal spores from damp organic storage sheds

explanation: Welding processes vaporize metals, producing hazardous fumes that cause acute or chronic respiratory irritation when inhaled in enclosed spaces. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is typically the earliest clinical symptom reported by a patient developing an occupational lung disease?

options.A: Exertional dyspnoea and a persistent dry cough
options.B: Severe pain radiating across the anterior chest wall
options.C: Complete loss of the sense of smell and taste
options.D: Sudden coughing up of bright red blood

explanation: Early lung tissue irritation and stiffness manifest first as shortness of breath during physical activity alongside a non-productive cough. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why is ruling out pulmonary tuberculosis an essential part of diagnostic evaluation for workers with suspected pneumoconiosis in high-burden regions?

options.A: Standard spirometry cannot be performed safely until active tuberculosis is fully treated
options.B: Tuberculosis causes identical finger clubbing that confuses the primary physical assessment
options.C: Chronic dust exposure suppresses local immunity, increasing vulnerability to tuberculosis co-infection
options.D: Tuberculosis bacteria completely reverse the fibrotic scarring caused by mineral dusts

explanation: Inhalation of dusts like silica impairs macrophage function, making the lungs a prime environment for secondary tuberculosis infections. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the single most critical intervention in the management of any occupational lung disease?

options.A: Immediate removal and cessation of exposure from the offending hazardous environment
options.B: Immediate initiation of long-term mechanical ventilation support
options.C: Surgical resection of the affected lower lobes of both lungs
options.D: Administration of high-dose systemic corticosteroids to reverse established fibrosis

explanation: Stopping further inhalation of the toxic agent is the only way to prevent continued inflammation and worsening of the condition. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h6)

question: A patient diagnosed with coal worker's pneumoconiosis is admitted to the medical ward complaining of worsening shortness of breath and fatigue. Which nursing intervention should be prioritized first?

options.A: Enrolling the patient in an intensive vocational retraining program for a new career
options.B: Administering broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics to prevent viral pneumonia
options.C: Assessing current oxygen saturation and administering supplemental oxygen as prescribed
options.D: Scheduling immediate diagnostic computed tomography of the chest

explanation: Stabilizing airway and gas exchange parameters through oxygenation takes clinical priority during acute worsening of respiratory distress. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h6)

question: What cardiac condition frequently develops as a late complication of chronic, severe pulmonary fibrosis?

options.A: Infective endocarditis affecting the mitral valve leaflets
options.B: Left ventricular hypertrophy caused by systemic arterial hypertension
options.C: Cor pulmonale resulting from increased vascular resistance in the lungs
options.D: Atherosclerotic coronary artery occlusion leading to myocardial infarction

explanation: Destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed raises blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries, forcing the right side of the heart to work harder. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why does long-term occupational exposure to asbestos carry a particularly poor prognosis compared to several other dust-related conditions?

options.A: It strongly predisposes individuals to aggressive malignancies such as malignant mesothelioma
options.B: It immediately causes total paralysis of the diaphragm muscle and respiratory arrest
options.C: It selectively destroys the heart muscle fibers within the first few weeks of contact
options.D: It prevents all forms of standard antibiotic treatment from reaching lung tissues

explanation: Asbestos fibers are potent carcinogens that significantly increase the lifetime risk of developing incurable lung cancers and mesotheliomas. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is considered the most effective approach to managing occupational lung diseases?

options.A: Primary prevention through eliminating or controlling workplace dust exposure
options.B: Routine administration of experimental anti-fibrotic medications to all workers
options.C: Early surgical lung transplantation once severe symptoms manifest
options.D: Mandatory retirement of workers after five years of industrial service

explanation: Preventing the disease from occurring in the first place by controlling hazardous exposures is far more effective than treating established damage. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h8)

question: Which responsibility is a core function of an occupational health nurse in a manufacturing setting?

options.A: Designing heavy industrial machinery to eliminate vibration hazards
options.B: Setting national minimum wage standards for industrial laborers
options.C: Performing complex thoracic surgical procedures on injured factory workers
options.D: Conducting periodic respiratory screenings and enforcing safety equipment compliance

explanation: Occupational health nurses monitor worker health through surveillance programs and promote adherence to workplace safety protocols. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h8)
